title: Where the application ends and the IT component begins
summary: One classification decision, made early and in writing, quietly decides whether your portfolio practice works for the next five years. The tests that settle the hard cases - SaaS, microservices, suites, middleware - and what the line unlocks, year by year, as the architecture function matures.
html:
Ask three people in the same IT organization how many applications the company runs and you will get three numbers, sometimes an order of magnitude apart. The difference is rarely about knowledge. It is about definition: one person counted the integration platform, the databases, and the job scheduler; one counted only what has a login screen; one counted whatever the license report spat out. All three are describing the same landscape.

This sounds like pedantry until you realize how much sits on top of that definition. It is one of the least glamorous decisions in enterprise architecture and one of the few that compounds - quietly, for years.

Every practice you want in year three is either enabled or poisoned by a classification you make in month one.

Composites from my own portfolio work, as always - blurred where it matters, precise where it helps.

Why the line carries so much weight#

An application and an IT component answer to different worlds. An application serves a business need: it processes business data, supports a process, and can be mapped to a business capability. It deserves a business owner, a business fit rating, and a place in the portfolio matrix. An IT component is what applications stand on - software, platforms, infrastructure, managed services. It deserves a technical custodian, an end-of-support date, and a place in the technology risk report.

Blur the two and every downstream practice inherits the blur. Your application count becomes a negotiation. Ownership campaigns stall, because no business owner will claim the message broker, and rightly so. Business fit and technical fit ratings turn to mush, because half the "applications" have no business users to rate them. Cost dashboards double-count - the platform and everything on it. And the obsolescence radar you want later never materializes, because end-of-support dates live on components you never modeled.

The application is what the business would miss by name. The component is what only the engineers would mourn.

Settling it before the arguments start#

The decision has to be made before mass collection begins, written into policy, and applied by people who are not architects - which means it has to be short. Three tests have served me well, applied in order:

Can you map it to a business capability without squinting? Would a named business owner accept accountability for it? If it vanished tonight, would the business notice it by name - or would they only notice things generally getting slower? Two yeses out of the first two make it an application. Only engineers mourning makes it a component.

Then pre-answer the edge cases, because they are always the same five. A SaaS product is an application and a component: the application carries the business relationship, a thin component placeholder underneath carries hosting, location, and cost. A microservice is an application only if it is a functional piece of the business landscape someone reuses; the runtime it ships in is a component. A suite gets two levels - the name a business user would say, with its modules as children - and resist anyone who wants a third level; I allow it only when a portal genuinely wraps independent apps. Middleware, databases, schedulers: components, always, no matter how expensive or beloved. And the spreadsheet running a process since 2014 is an application in denial - inventory it as one, or it stays invisible until it breaks.

Write the rule and the edge cases on one page. Not a modeling handbook - one page, with examples from your own landscape. The test of the policy is whether a project manager filling in a form gets it right without calling you.

What happens next, year by year#

The payoff schedule is remarkably predictable. I have watched it play out - and I have watched its mirror image where the line stayed blurry.

Year one is the unglamorous one: a reclassification wave, some bruised feelings when someone's system is "demoted" to component, and then - counts that stop moving. The dashboard number means the same thing in March and in November. That alone changes the tone of portfolio meetings.

Year two, technical fit ratings become real, because components now carry lifecycle and end-of-support dates and applications inherit the risk through their stack. The first honest technology risk report appears: which business applications stand on dying technology. That report is unwritable in a blurred inventory.

Year three, money. Cost and licensing attach to components; business value attaches to applications; the two stop being double-counted in the same slide. Application rationalization and technology refresh become two roadmaps that reference each other instead of one confused backlog fighting itself for budget.

Years four and five are where the compounding shows. Impact analysis becomes a query, not a workshop: which applications are touched if we retire that platform version - minutes, with confidence. Security and audit start consuming the same tree instead of building their own shadow inventories. And the model survives people leaving, because the line is written down rather than lived in someone's head.

The mirror timeline is shorter to tell: year one, arguments about the count; year two, ratings nobody trusts; year three, a cost report that gets quietly withdrawn; year five, a new CIO orders a re-inventory from zero, and the cycle restarts with fresh optimism. I have been part of that restart. It is funded with the same money that the one-page rule would have cost, multiplied by roughly ten.

The tests, on one hand#

Capability: can you map it to one without squinting. Owner: would a business person claim it. Absence: who notices when it is gone, and do they know its name. SaaS is both, suite is two levels, middleware is always a component. And the whole thing fits on one page - if your classification policy needs a training course, it is not a policy, it is a hobby.

Draw the line once, early, in writing. Then let it be boring. The most valuable classification decision in the portfolio is the one nobody has argued about since the quarter it was made.
